# How Strategic Incentives Affect Interbranch Representation {#sec-results-incentives}

> ABSTRACT: How does the political environment shape the strategic incentives for legislators to engage in interbranch representation? In this chapter we explore how it shapes decisions about *how much* interbranch representation, *what type* of interbranch activity (policy or constituency service), and on *whose behalf* legislators work (constituents, companies, nonprofits or local governments). We find that interbranch representation is shaped by partisan/ideological, electoral, and institutional incentives, and may work through the mechanism of staff allocation. Generally, we find alignment (working with allies) outweighs antagonism in shaping interbranch representation. On the electoral side, we see competitive general elections help select House members who do more constituency service, while it is competitive primaries that induce individual house members to change they behavior. 

```{r, include=FALSE, cache=FALSE}
# formatting for tables and numbers
here::here("code", "formatting.R") |> source()
type = "total"
```


In @sec-results-demand and @sec-results-capacity, we examined the first two elements of our framework of interbranch representation: constituent demand and member office capacity. We found that sources of constituent demand (*number*, *empowerment* and *needs* of constituents) appear to shape the interbranch representation work done by congressional offices---particularly so for constituency service, which often needs to be originated by a constituent. We believe these sources of constituent demand shape how much expressed demand (requests for help from constituents) reaches congressional offices. Our second element, *capacity*, shapes how much of that work offices are able to do. But constituent demand and office capacity alone are insufficient to explain variation in interbranch representation. Legislators facing similar demands, with similar resources, still differ considerably in which agencies they contact, about what (constituency service or policy), and on whose behalf. These differences reflect political choices legislators make about how to allocate their time, effort, and staff resources. Unlike most legislative work, which is often constrained by the number of seats a legislator's party holds in Congress or the party's agenda, interbranch representation is largely at each office’s discretion, which makes it an unusually clear window into legislators’ unconstrained (or less constrained) behavior.

In this chapter we examine the third element of our framework: *strategic incentives*. @hyp-strategy (strategic incentives), introduced in @sec-theory, expects that the political environment shapes the strategic choices legislators make about how much, and what kinds of, interbranch representation to do. As @fig-strategy-flowchart shows, demand and capacity set the conditions under which offices act, while partisan, electoral, and institutional incentives shape what activities legislators pursue and on whose behalf. Offices’ staff allocations, in turn, reflect these choices and help carry them out.


```{r}
#| label: fig-strategy-flowchart
#| fig-cap: "How strategic incentives shape interbranch representation."
#| out-width: "85%"
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "causal-strategy.png"))
```

Strategic incentives differ from demand and capacity in an important way. We expect more demand and more capacity to increase interbranch representation, but strategic incentives can push in different directions. Partisan incentives, for example, could lead legislators to work more with agencies run by their allies, which would be a form of collaborative interbranch work. Alternatively, legislators could work more with agencies run by their opponents---a form of oversight or combative interbranch work. In the sections that follow, we develop sub-hypotheses for each of the three sources of strategic incentives (partisan and ideological, electoral, and institutional), and we test them using the same models as in the previous chapters. 

We follow those analyses with an examination of a mechanism of how legislators turn priorities into interbranch work: how legislators choose to strategically allocate their staff across constituent vs. policy-focused roles. We descriptively examine those allocation choices, and then examine whether and how staff allocation decisions translate into the provision of different forms of interbranch representation. <!---In a future revision we could also use staff allocation decisions as a DV, and look at how our strategic incentives shape those allocation decisions. ---> 

We find that strategic incentives shape whose interests legislators represent more than how much interbranch representation they do. Republicans do more constituency service for individuals and businesses, while Democrats do more work on behalf of nonprofits and local governments and more general policy work. Legislators who share the president's party do more work on behalf of nonprofits and local governments. Ideological distance from an agency works in different ways for different types of interbranch representation: legislators do more work on behalf of nonprofits and local governments when they are closer to an agency but more corporate policy work when they are ideologically more distant from an agency. Electoral competition, by contrast, has little consistent relationship with interbranch representation. Majority status also has complicated effects, made even more complex by its strong correlation with committee chair status. Controlling for committee chair status, House members that experience a change---their party becomes the majority---do less individual constituency service, less nonprofit and local government service, and less interbranch representation overall. They do however, do more general policy work, though that dynamic primarily works through committee chairs, and is more attenuated for backbench majority party members.  <!---[Add majority additional findings once Devin’s figures are in.] Rochelle 11/14: I added these last two sentences but idk if there's more we want to say about majority status---> 

## Three Sources of Strategic Incentives

Unlike capacity, which we expect to have a positive relationship with interbranch representation, strategic incentives can push legislators toward more or less of this work, and toward some kinds of work and constituents rather than others. We consider three features of the political environment that may shape legislators’ strategic incentives about interbranch representation: (1) partisan and ideological features, (2) electoral features, and (3) institutional features. 

### Partisanship and Ideology

::: {#hyp-strategy-partisan .hypothesis name="Partisan"}
The partisan and ideological environment shapes how much and what kinds of interbranch representation legislators do. These incentives could push in opposite directions, depending on whether interbranch work is mainly collaborative or adversarial.
:::

If interbranch work focuses on procuring benefits for constituents, we should see more work among partisan and ideological allies. For example, members of the president's party receive more federal spending in their districts [@BerryBurdenHowell2010]. Expecting relatively greater success, members of the president's party may thus engage in higher levels of interbranch representation. Interbranch representation is at the nexus of the Congress and the executive branch. The behavior we are documenting in this book is the congressional portion of that relationship; it is legislators reaching out to executive branch agencies. To actually deliver results to their constituents, the agencies need to cooperate. If legislators of the president's party think they are more likely to receive higher levels of cooperation from executive branch agencies, they may be motivated to attempt interbranch representation at higher rates.

::: {#hyp-strategy-partisan-alignment .hypothesis name="Alignment"}
Legislators from the president's party will do more interbranch representation, and legislators who are ideologically closer to an agency will do more interbranch representation with that agency.
:::

A similar logic of working with friends and receiving a warmer reception applies for agencies that are ideologically closer to the legislators. This may be in part because of the way that party coalitions represent interests. For example, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) may be perceived as conservative in part because it represents Republican-dominated rural states, and the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) may be perceived as liberal because it represents more urbanized states dominated by Democrats. If interbranch work is about procuring benefits, we would expect rural representatives to work more with USDA and urban representatives to work more with HUD, thus producing a pattern of interbranch work favoring allies in one's policymaking and implementing coalition.

Alternatively, if interbranch work focuses more on oversight than procuring benefits for constituents, we might see the opposite. While members of the president's party might anticipate a friendlier reception from executive branch agencies controlled by a same-party president, members of the opposition party might have greater incentives to engage in oversight of an executive branch controlled by an opposing party's president [but see @Lowande2018APSR]. Similarly, we might anticipate constituents of opposition party legislators having more concerns or problems with agencies more associated with a president of a different party, who might prioritize different types of constituents or policies less hospitable to opposition party constituents. Lastly, Ritchie's argument that legislators turn to backdoor policymaking when they confront obstacles in the legislative process applies here, too. Faced with a president unlikely to support the legislative proposals of opposition legislators, Ritchie found that legislators were more likely to turn to backchannel policymaking [@Ritchie2023].

::: {#hyp-strategy-partisan-antagonism .hypothesis name="Antagonism"}
Legislators from the party opposing the president will do more interbranch representation, and legislators who are ideologically more distant from an agency will do more interbranch representation with that agency.
:::

Party coalitions suggest some divergence with respect to which constituencies legislators represent, with Republicans typically perceived as being friendlier to business interests [@GimpelLeeParrott2014]. Ideology may also matter for legislators' interbranch representation, as more bipartisan (and therefore more ideologically moderate, per DW-NOMINATE scores) legislators are more effective at pursuing their policymaking goals through lawmaking [@HarbridgeVoldenWiseman2023].


::: {#hyp-strategy-partisan-coalition .hypothesis name="Business coalition"}
Republicans will do more interbranch representation on behalf of businesses.
:::

The same logic could apply to interbranch representation, with more ideologically extreme legislators doing less of this work. In the last few decades, the Republican party has shifted to the right, with a particular focus on smaller government [@GrossmannHopkins2016]. This dynamic has been especially pronounced in its more extreme Tea Party and Freedom Caucus wings in recent years [@Blum2020; @Green2019; @Lee2026]. A notable focus of these factions has been on reducing the size of the federal government and attacking the very existence of the administrative state [@Metzger2017; @SkowronekDearbornKing2021; @Moynihan2022]. For these reasons we might imagine Tea Party and Freedom Caucus Republicans to be *less* likely to engage in interbranch representation. Because ideologically extreme Democrats generally favor *more* government action and involvement, we would not expect to see such an effect for all ideologically extreme legislators.

::: {#hyp-strategy-partisan-antigovernment .hypothesis name="Anti-government"}
Tea Party and Freedom Caucus Republicans will do less interbranch representation.
:::

### Electoral Incentives

::: {#hyp-strategy-electoral .hypothesis name="Electoral"}
Electoral incentives shape how much and what kinds of interbranch representation legislators do, both directly and through the fundraising that electoral competition demands.
:::

While it is difficult to measure a legislator's incentive structure directly, we can identify situations in which legislators are likely to prioritize certain goals. Perhaps the most widely recognized strategic incentive of legislators is reelection [e.g., @Mayhew1974; @CainFerejohnFiorina1987; @Fiorina1977; @Fenno1973]. As David Mayhew famously wrote in *Congress: The Electoral Connection*, "\[Reelection\] has to be the *proximate* goal of everyone, the goal that must be achieved over and over if other ends are to be entertained" [@Mayhew1974, pg. 16]. Legislators motivated by electoral concerns might devote additional attention and resources to helping their constituents, so that those constituents will vote to reelect the legislator [@Dodd1977; @Fiorina1977; @CainFerejohnFiorina1987; @SerraCover1992; @SerraMoon1994; @DroppPeskowitz2012]. Yet, in the modern Congress, very few members of Congress are electorally vulnerable in either general or primary elections. Legislators who do find themselves in an electorally vulnerable political environment are likely to prioritize reelection. 

Members of Congress purport to believe that constituency service work will help their reelection efforts, with 44% of members saying they believed reelection was the primary reason most members perform constituency service [@Johannes1984, pg. 13]. This intuition has some empirical grounding. In their exploration of why Americans like their individual member of Congress more than Congress the institution (what has become known as "Fenno's paradox"), @ParkerDavidson1979 found that Americans evaluate the institution of Congress based on its legislative performance, the style and pace of the legislative process, and legislative-executive relations. At the same time, they judge individual members of Congress on the basis of two factors: constituency service and the legislator's personal characteristics.

This expectation that electorally vulnerable legislators will do more constituency service, however, is contrary to Ritchie's findings in *Backdoor Lawmaking* about a different form of interbranch representation---policy work with federal agencies---which showed no consistent relationship between electoral vulnerability and policy work with federal agencies [@Ritchie2023].

Another potential reason for caution regarding the relationship between electoral vulnerability and interbranch representation is the invisibility of interbranch representation. Although reelection motives have long been posited as a motivation to engage in constituency service, a skeptic might question whether allocating time and resources to a largely invisible activity rather than something more visible like communications or legislation is the best strategy. While acts of constituency service might be visible to an individual who has been helped, as well as their friends and family, one would have to assume fairly large social network amplification effects for it to reach enough voters to make an electoral difference at a time when the size of the average House district is over 760,000 people [@CRSCensus2026].

::: {#hyp-strategy-electoral-competition .hypothesis name="Electoral competition"}
Legislators whose prior general or primary election was competitive will do more interbranch representation.
:::

Thus far, we have focused on how electoral motivations could drive legislators to focus more on constituent concerns. We could think of this as legislators *responding* to an electoral threat by working harder for constituents when they are scared of losing their seats [@Mayhew1974; @Fiorina1977]. An alternative mechanism that could explain electorally vulnerable legislators doing more interbranch representation is *selection*. In a selection-based story, legislators who hold competitive seats may differ from those who hold safe seats. A robust formal theory literature considers the role that elections (voters and parties) play in selecting high-quality candidates [@Ashworth2012]. @GalassoNannicini2011 examine whether electoral competition is good for political selection, presenting both a formal model and empirical results from the Italian parliament. They find, consistent with their model's predictions, that higher quality candidates are more likely to run in competitive districts and politicians elected in competitive districts perform better in the sense that they have fewer absences. These differences are due to selection more than to reelection incentives. If competitive elections select higher quality legislators, then we may observe a relationship between electoral competition, and interbranch representation for reasons other than as a response to reelection concerns. An alternative relationship could also exist: higher quality politicians who provide more constituency services (among other performance indicators) could deter strong challenges, so that a reputation for high-quality performance could help contribute to larger electoral margins. Indeed, the work of @Fiorina1977 and others who have argued that constituency service contributes to the incumbency advantage may suggest exactly that.  

Our two different types of models---the within-legislator models and the across-legislator models---may help us disentangle these complex relationships. Comparisons across legislators cannot distinguish response from selection. Comparing the same legislator before and after their seat becomes competitive, however, can make this distinction, because it holds constant the politician's quality.  

**Corporate fundraising** Legislators also choose on whose behalf to advocate. Research on campaign contributions has generally found that money does not buy roll call votes [@AnsFigSny03], but highly visible votes may be one of the least desirable channels of influence [@PowellGrimmer2015]. The relative invisibility of interbranch representation may make it a more attractive pathway for the influence of campaign contributions [@PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023]. In a study of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, @PowellJudgeLordGrimmer2023 found that legislators who received more contributions from energy company PACs did more interbranch advocacy on behalf of corporate interests.

::: {#hyp-strategy-electoral-donors .hypothesis name="Corporate donors"}
Legislators who receive more corporate PAC contributions will do more interbranch representation on behalf of businesses (corporate constituency service and corporate policy work).
:::


<!--- Commenting out fundraising as distraction. We kind of look at this in conclusion. Leaving out for now.
At the same time, conventional wisdom holds that the more time legislators spend "dialing for dollars," the less time they and their offices have for constituency service and policy work.

::: {#hyp-strategy-electoral-distraction .hypothesis name="Fundraising as distraction"}
Legislators who receive more corporate PAC contributions will do less interbranch representation.
:::
---> 

### Institutional Incentives

A central form of institutional advantage is being a member of the majority party, in which it is easier to achieve legislative goals. Thus, legislators who are in the majority may invest more in legislative work, which may result in their doing less interbranch representation. In her research on backdoor policymaking with federal agencies, Ritchie argues that legislators are most likely to turn to backchannel lawmaking by appealing directly to federal agencies when they face obstacles in the legislative process [@Ritchie2023]. Majority legislators encounter a much friendlier legislative environment and are thus less likely than minority legislators to turn to backchannel policy appeals to bureaucratic agencies. 


::: {#hyp-strategy-institutional .hypothesis name="Institutional"}
Legislators in the majority party will do less interbranch representation.
:::

### Mechanism: Staff Allocation

The last strategic choice that we consider is how legislators allocate their staff. Where @sec-results-capacity examined how many staff an office has, here we consider how offices divide them across different tasks. Legislators who choose to prioritize a certain type of activity may want to devote more staff resources to accomplish that objective [@Reynolds2020]. Thus, we can view staff allocation choices (in the form of the amount of a legislator’s office budget that they spend on constituency service staff, for instance) as a reflection of the member’s priorities, and thus a strategic choice they are making. We argue that member offices that devote more resources to staff who do a certain type of work are likely to produce more of that type of work.

::: {#hyp-strategy-staff .hypothesis name="Staff allocation"}
Offices that allocate more staff to a type of work will do more of that type of interbranch representation.
:::

## Measuring Strategic Incentives

Legislators may strategically respond to their political environment in a number of ways, some of which may affect how they allocate their office capacity. As measurements of strategic behavior, we rely on legislators' staff allocation, ideological distance from federal agencies, electoral competitiveness, majority party status, and whether the legislator is a member of the president's party. The latter four factors are features of the political environment to which legislators are likely to respond strategically, while legislators' choices about staff allocation likely *reflect* strategic choices about the kind of work that they wish to prioritize. 

To assess the ideological similarity between members of Congress and each federal agency, we compare members' first dimension
DW-NOMINATE scores [@dwnominate2024] with survey-based measurements of federal
agencies' perceived ideological leanings [@RichardsonClintonLewis2018].
To measure the ideological *distance* between members of Congress and
federal agencies, we subtract each member’s first-dimension DW-NOMINATE
score from the ideology score of each agency.^[
Technically, 0 has no special meaning on these latent scales; therefore, for example, there is no reason that -1 and 1 are equally ideologically distant. However, the @RichardsonClintonLewis2018 scale is locally identified to have mean 0, so absolute value serves as a linear measure of distance from the mean. Moreover, agencies with ideological scores near zero include the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), and Veterans Benefits Administration (VBA), which are agencies that respondents presumably would perceive to be neither liberal nor conservative when responding to the survey question, suggesting 0 could be considered "moderate." @RichardsonClintonLewis2018 estimates subagency-specific perceived ideology scores for many sub-agencies in our data. For sub-agencies that do not have a specific score, we use their department's score. 
Six small, extremely low-salience independent agencies or commissions do not have a score. We assign them a score of 0. <!--This makes the measure of distance for these agencies the same as the absolute value of a member's first-dimension DW-NOMINATE score, which we control for in all models.-->  These six were 
the American Battle Monuments Commission (ABMC), 
the Court Services and Offender Supervision Agency (CSOSA),
National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC; despite making the news in 2026, it is reasonable to assume it did not have a strong partisan perception prior),
U.S. Nuclear Waste Technical Review Board, 
the Postal Regulatory Commission (PRC), and the U.S. Railroad Retirement Board (RRB)
]
For example, Bernie Sanders, with a NOMINATE score of -0.545 (liberal), has a distance close to zero with the Department of Labor's Mine Health and Safety Administration with a score of -0.580 (liberal), but a distance close to 1 with the United States Trade Representative (USTR) with a score of 0.439 (conservative). 
The largest distance in our data is 2.66 between the Office of the Secretary of Defense and Joint Staff (1.91) and Carte Goodwin (-0.747).
To help guard against conclusions about distance being driven by distance from zero on the DW-NOMINATE scale, we control for the absolute value of the first dimension of DW-NOMINATE. 
 We also use other legislator-level variables from @dwnominate2024, including party membership to derive majority status and whether a legislator is a member of the president's party. 

To test @hyp-strategy-partisan-antigovernment, we measure Freedom Caucus and Tea Party membership by using a cut point of a DW-NOMINATE score of 0.5 and above. While this is not exactly the same as caucus party membership, we believe it captures most members of these factions, and has the advantage of being a consistent measure over time. These actual caucus memberships do not exist for our entire time period and evolve beyond their creation, changing names from Tea Party to Freedom Caucus. Thus, the NOMINATE-based measure lets us measure this faction of very conservative legislators in a more stable way over time.

For data on electoral competitiveness, we start with data from @Thomsen2023 on vote share in primary and general elections, adopting her definition of whether an election was competitive. For general election competitiveness, we fill in gaps in the @Thomsen2023 data by applying a similar decision rule (whether the winner received less than 57.5% of the vote) to vote share data compiled by @VoldenWiseman2014 and @VoldenWiseman2018. Notably, the average percent of members of Congress whose prior election was competitive (weighted by the number of agencies for which we have data for that year) was 30% for general elections and 10% for primary elections (House only). The number of districts that change from non-competitive to competitive is even smaller, possibly frustrating tests for the effect of electoral competitiveness. 

To measure corporate fundraising, we use the total contributions each legislator received from corporate political action committees in the prior Congress [DEVIN: source]. For the Department of Energy case study, we use contributions from energy sector PACs specifically.

<!--Rochelle 11/14: we mention above that we use DW-NOMINATE data for majority party status -->
For @hyp-strategy-institutional, we use an indicator for whether a legislator’s party held the majority in their chamber in that Congress, derived from party membership in @dwnominate2024.

To measure staff allocation, we use the number of staffers working in casework positions in each legislator’s personal office based on LegiStorm’s staff titles [@Legistorm].

## Results

<!-- DEVIN: Please confirm or correct the bracketed details:
(1) same model, unit, and clustering as Chapters 5 and 6?
(2) specify controls in these models (demand and capacity measures?), and fixed effects in the within-legislator models;
(3) appendix table references. -->

To estimate how strategic incentives relate to interbranch representation, we use the same approach as in @sec-results-demand and @sec-results-capacity: we model the number of contacts of each type that a legislator's office makes with each federal agency in a given year, using negative binomial regressions with standard errors clustered by legislator. Each model includes all of the strategic incentive measures together, along with controls for demand and capacity. 

Where possible, we again estimate both cross-sectional and within-legislator models. Some strategic incentives change over a legislator's career: legislators gain or lose a co-partisan president, move between the majority and minority, and face more or less competitive elections. For these, within-legislator models compare the same legislator before and after the change. Others rarely or never change within a legislator's career, including party and ideology, so for these we rely on cross-sectional comparisons. Few districts change from safe to competitive, which limits what within-legislator models can tell us about electoral competition. Because cross-sectional comparisons cannot rule out that legislators who face different incentives also differ in other ways, we interpret these results more cautiously than the within-legislator estimates in @sec-results-capacity.

As in the previous chapters, we report the percent difference in expected contacts associated with each indicator (or with a one standard deviation increase, for continuous measures such as ideological distance, PAC contributions, and staff shares). In each figure, points mark the estimated effect for total interbranch representation and each of the five types of interbranch representation and horizontal lines show 95% confidence intervals. Panel labels indicate whether estimates are cross-sectional or within-legislator and whether they come from House, Senate, or pooled models. Full results are in [DEVIN: appendix table reference].


### Partisan and Ideological Allies Mostly Work Together

Partisan and ideological incentives drive interbranch work in several ways (@hyp-strategy-partisan). Rather than full support for all partisan and ideological sub-hypotheses, we find different parts of @hyp-strategy-partisan supported for different kinds of interbranch work. 

#### Presidential Alignment, Not Antagonism 

We begin by considering the countervailing pressures of alignment (@hyp-strategy-partisan-alignment) and antagonism (@hyp-strategy-partisan-antagonism) for members of the president's party. @fig-marginal-presidentparty shows the marginal effect of being a member of the president's party, all else held equal, on interbranch representation. Overall, we see support for alignment outweighing antagonism: members of the president's party engage in approximately 3.5% more total interbranch representation in the diff-in-diff models.^[In this case we see very similar patterns of results in the cross-sectional and diff-in-diff models, though a few coefficients that are significant in the diff-in-diff fail to reach conventional levels of significance in the cross-sectional models.] If we dive into the sub-types of interbranch representation, we mostly see a similar pattern with the president's co-partisans doing more, though the effect size varies from a low of 4% for individual constituent service to a high of 28% for nonprofit and local government service. Notably, the sole exception to this alignment story is for general policy work, where the point estimate is negative (-1%), though it fails to reach conventional levels of statistical significance. That the alignment hypothesis fails in precisely the category---general policy work---where we might see traditional forms of congressional oversight suggests that our traditional understanding of adversarial antagonism may play a role there. 


```{r}
#| label: fig-marginal-presidentparty
#| fig-cap: "Marginal effect of being a member of the president's party on interbranch representation. Points show the estimated percent difference in each type of interbranch representation associated with being a member of the president's party with 95% confidence intervals. The upper panel shows cross-sectional estimates and the lower panel shows within-legislator estimates." 
#| fig-alt: "Marginal effects of sharing the president's party on interbranch representation"
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-presidents_party-1.png"))

```


#### Agency Antagonism and Alignment 

In the last section, we examined how partisan alignment between a legislator and the presidency influenced interbranch representation. Another way to think about those results is thinking about the presidency as influencing everything in the executive branch; therefore, legislators who agree or disagree with the presidency would act differently overall. A different approach to considering alignment or antagonism looks at agency-specific ideology measures---for example, even under the same president, the Department of Defense is viewed as more conservative than the Environmental Protection Agency. Here we examine what happens when a district elects a representative that is more distant from the perceived ideology of the agency. Do more ideologically distant legislators appear to act as antagonists, increasing their interbranch representation (@hyp-strategy-partisan-antagonism), or do we see more activity from ideologically proximate legislators acting as aligned allies (@hyp-strategy-partisan-alignment)? 

Legislators' engaging more with agencies that they perceived as ideologically similar or distant is more about *which* agencies representatives target, rather than *how much* they do overall. @fig-marginal-ideodist shows the marginal effect of a one standard deviation increase in a legislator's ideological distance from an agency.^[We can only estimate the cross-sectional model here, because we lack enough variation to estimate the diff-in-diff.] We see no difference in individual constituency service or corporate service, where we find fairly precisely estimated zeros. But we see opposite alignment vs. antagonism patterns for our other forms of interbranch representation. General policy work (-16%), nonprofit/local government service (-15%), and total interbranch representation (-6.5%) follow a pattern of *alignment*, where more ideologically similar legislators do more work with the agency. On the antagonism side, we see more ideologically distant legislators engage in substantially more corporate policy work (+28%). This suggests that legislative offices may be doing policy work on behalf of certain industries by attacking regulators of those industries (e.g., conservatives spending time representing industry interests to the Environmental Protection Agency, which is perceived as ideologically distant). 


```{r}
#| label: fig-marginal-ideodist
#| fig-cap: "Marginal efffect of ideological alignment with agency on interbranch representation. Points show the estimated percent difference in each type of interbranch representation associated with one standard deviation greater perceived ideological distance from the agency, with 95% confidence intervals. We show cross-sectional estimates only, because legislators' ideology rarely changes over their careers."
#| fig-alt: "Marginal effects of ideological distance from an agency on five types of interbranch representation"
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-distance-1.png"))
```


#### Conservative Business Coalition Supports Corporate Service, but Not Corporate Policy

As expected, Republicans do significantly more corporate constituency service (@fig-marginal-party)---nearly 40% more than Democrats on average. Interestingly, Republicans do not do significantly more policy work on behalf of businesses, though the effect is in the expected positive direction (9% more than Democrats). We estimate these effects using cross-sectional models only, because there are not enough legislators who switched parties to allow us to identify within-legislator effects. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-marginal-party
#| fig-cap: "Marginal effect of party on interbranch representatin. Points show the estimated percent difference in each type of interbranch representation for Republicans compared with Democrats, with 95% confidence intervals, from cross-sectional models."
#| fig-alt: "Marginal effects of Republican party membership on five types of interbranch representation"
#| out-width: "70%"

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-party-1.png"))
```

We had no expectations for the effect of partisanship on total interbranch representation, and indeed, Republicans and Democrats do not significantly differ in their overall levels of interbranch representation. We did not have theoretical expectations for party differences in our other subtypes of interbranch representation, but we did find significant party differences in our three other categories: individual constituency service, nonprofit and local government constituency service, and general policy work. Notably, we find holding all else equal, Republicans do significantly more individual constituency service than Democrats (27%), while Democrats do significantly more nonprofit/local government service and more general policy work (both around 18% more). 

We do not have an explanation for why we find Republicans doing so much more individual constituency service work, but there are several possibilities. One comes from the fact that Republicans tend to do more individual constituency service on behalf of veterans and seniors [@SnyderJudgeLordPowellGrimmer2025]---a pattern which could translate into the partisan difference we observe here because of the amount of individual constituency service work that involves veterans and seniors through the VA and the Social Security Administration. However, the large volume of individual constituency service on behalf of immigrants contained in our data makes this explanation unlikely. <!--ROCHELLE 11/14: is that true??? how do agency fixed effects affect that interpretation? --> Another related possibility is that Republicans' anti-government ethos does not extend to the parts of the administrative state that support their policy goals, especially those that maintain the status of relatively powerful groups and institutions, like the military and law enforcement. A third potential explanation is that Republicans do more constituency service not in spite of their anti-government preferences, but *because* of them. In other words, Republicans may wish to claim credit for helping constituents solve problems with a government that they view as broken and wasteful. The fact that constituency service often involves helping individuals recover money from the federal government---a highly individualized form of "saving taxpayer money"---lends credence to this explanation. <!-- We speculate that one possibility is that lower cost of living in districts represented by Republicans, may allow Republicans being able to hire more district staff despite allocating the same share of their budget, on average, to constituency service.  If we want to make this claim, we should probably test it with our staff budget info?--> Ultimately, however, these results are unable to tell us whether this partisan difference is a function of something about the Republican Party as an institution or instead a function of the parties' orientations toward the role of government. To parse this result further, we next test our hypothesis about Tea Party/Freedom Caucus members specifically. 


#### Anti-government legislators do less policy work and more individual service 

@fig-marginal-antigovernment compares the legislators on the far right end of the ideological spectrum, often but not always members of the Tea Party or Freedom Caucuses within the Republican Party, to all other legislators in their provision of interbranch representation. Consistent with our expectations, legislators on the extreme ideological end of the Republican party in both chambers do far less nonprofit and local government service (House: -20%, Senate: -31%), and general policy work (House: -17%, Senate: -27%) with federal agencies than their peers. On the Senate side, we see that same pattern of significant decreases hold for corporate policy (Senate: -21%) and total interbranch representation (-18%). 

```{r}
#| label: fig-marginal-antigovernment
#| fig-cap: "Marginal Effect of Anti-government ideology on interbranch representation. Points show the estimated percent difference in each type of interbranch representation for Antigovernment legislators compared to all other legislators, with 95% confidence intervals, from cross-sectional models."
#| fig-alt: "Marginal effects of antigovernment legislators on five types of interbranch representation"
#| out-width: "70%"

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-far_right-2.png"))
```

More surprisingly, we see House members on the far right do substantially more individual constituency service (House: +24%). We do not have an empirical explanation for this pattern, though we note its consistent with what we observed for all Republicans (+27) and may be driven by what we explained above: anti-government legislators may view individual constituency service as an opportunity to point out broad problems with the federal government that accord with their ideological views. On the Senate side, we see no significant impact of more ideologically extreme Republicans on individual constituency service, where the point estimate is -7%, and fails to rise to conventional levels of statistical significance.  

Turning to corporate service, we see that far-right House members do substantially more corporate service work than their peers (+31%). The corporate service increase is less surprising given our previous hypothesis and finding about the Republican Party overall being more supportive of corporate interests. And, indeed, though the results are not significant in the Senate, we find a point estimate of an increase of 13% there. 


### Electoral Results

We turn next to considering what has long been considered the canonical motivation behind constituency service: electoral incentives (@hyp-strategy-electoral). We first consider the relationship between competitive elections (general and primary) and interbranch representation. We then turn to considering the impact of corporate PAC contributions of corporate forms on interbranch representation (service and policy). We look at the overall relationship between corporate PAC contributions and interbranch representation and then consider a case study of energy PAC contributions on energy interbranch representation. 

#### Competitive General Elections May Select House Members, and Competitive Primaries May Change Them

@fig-marginal-electoral shows differences across chambers and across model specification in the relationship between electoral competitiveness and interbranch representation. Legislators could face electoral pressure at either the primary or general election stage. @fig-marginal-electoral-1 shows the impact of a prior competitive general election, while @fig-marginal-electoral-2 shows the impact of a prior competitive primary election. We start by considering the impact of electoral competition for House members. If we look across members, we find that House members whose prior general election was competitive do about 12% more constituency service for individuals and 15% more for businesses than members in safe seats (@fig-marginal-electoral-1). But when we look to the within-member House model, we see that when the same House member's seat becomes competitive in the general election, their constituency service does not increase (@fig-marginal-electoral-1, House diff-in-diff panel). This pattern is consistent with the idea that competitive House districts might help *select* legislators who do more constituency service, rather than competition changing legislator behavior. However, the primary election results tell a slightly different story, where we see no differences cross-sectionally for competitive primaries but do find effects in the difference-in-difference models. Here we see that close primaries may push legislators to do 14% more individual constituency service in the next congress---evidence consistent with the idea that legislators are responding to competitive electoral environments. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-marginal-electoral
#| fig-cap: "Marginal Effect of Electoral Competitiveness on interbranch representation. "
#| out-width: "100%"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "Competitive General Election"
#|   - "Competitive Primary Election"

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-competitive-1.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-competitive_primary-1.png"))
```


More puzzling for all election-based stories are the Senate results, where we see no positive impacts of electoral competitiveness on any form of interbranch representation regardless of model specification (within or between legislators). On the Senate side, we actually see a very different story where competitive seats are associated with *less* work on behalf of nonprofits and local governments (-21%) and total interbranch representation (-10%), but this difference disappears within legislators. 

#### Legislators who receive more corporate PAC money do more corporate interbranch representation, but corporate PAC money does not change their behavior

Next we examine the impact of corporate PAC campaign contributions on corporate forms of interbranch representation (@fig-marginal-pac). The upper panel shows the cross-sectional model, while the lower panel shows the diff-in-diff model for all legislators. The panels show the impact of a one standard deviation increase in PAC contributions. Consistent with our expectations, in the cross-sectional model we see that legislators who receive more corporate PAC money do more corporate interbranch representation (4% corporate service, and 3.8% corporate policy), though those effect sizes are modest. It is also worth noting that those legislators who receive more corporate money appear to do slightly more of all forms of interbranch representation. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-marginal-pac
#| fig-cap: "Marginal Effect of Corporate PAC contributions on interbranch representation. Points show the estimated percent difference of a one standard devision difference in corporate PAC contributions, with 95% confidence intervals, from cross-sectional models."
#| fig-alt: "Marginal effects of corporate PAC contributions on five types of interbranch representation"
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-pac-1.png"))
```

A tricky question is whether corporate PAC money appears to change legislators' behavior. Here our within-legislator diff-in-diff model can speak to this question. We see no support for corporate PAC money changing legislators' corporate interbranch behavior (a fairly precisely estimated 0.0% point estimate for corporate service, and an insignificant 1.1% increase for corporate policy). Surprisingly, in the diff-in-diff model we actually see legislators doing modestly more individual constituency service (2.0%). 

#### Case Study: Energy PAC Campaign Contributions and Corporate Constituency Service to the Department of Energy

Instead of just considering the impact of all corporate PAC contributions on corporate interbranch representation, here we turn to a case study of corporate constituency service directed toward the Department of Energy. By focusing on work with a single agency, we can look more specifically at campaign contributions the legislator received from the energy sector political action committees, as opposed to the total corporate PAC contributions we examined in the previous section and models. We think this more specific test is a better test of the hypothesis. 

@fig-marginal-energypac-1 shows the impact of a one standard deviation increase in energy PAC contributions on interbranch contacts with the Department of Energy, while @fig-marginal-energypac-2 shows the impact of a one standard deviation increase in PAC contributions from non-energy PACs on interbranch contacts with the Department of Energy. Our donor impact hypothesis would suggest there should be a relationship between energy PAC contributions, but not non-energy PAC contributions, and Department of Energy contacts. The results largely support that pattern. Looking cross-sectionally, we see legislators who receive more energy PAC contributions do more corporate service (10%), corporate policy (37%), general policy (32%), and total interbranch (13%) work with the Department of Energy. If we then turn to our more rigorous diff-in-diff model to look at change in behavior within legislators, we see that receiving more energy sector PAC contributions results in more general policy work (19%) and total interbranch representation (12%) with the agency. Somewhat surprisingly, we see no significant effects for corporate policy or corporate service, though the effects are in the expected direction. 


```{r}
#| label: fig-marginal-energypac
#| fig-cap: "Marginal effect of Energy PAC contributions on interbranch contacts with the Department of Energy. Points show the estimated percent difference of a one standard deviation increase in Energy PAC contributions, with 95% confidence intervals, from cross-sectional models."
#| fig-alt: "Marginal effects of Energy PAC contributions on contact with Department of Energy"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "Energy PAC"
#|   - "Placebo: Non Energy PAC "

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-pac_energy-1.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-pac_nonenergy-1.png"))
```

For non-energy PAC contributions---analogous to a placebo in this case--- we see no increases in interbranch representation with the Department of Energy. The sole significant finding is a large decrease in policy work, though we note that there is a wide confidence interval there, and relatively little of that work in this case. 


### Institutional 

We consider institutional incentives through the lens of majority and minority status (@hyp-strategy-institutional). We expect members of the majority party to do less interbranch representation because they are better able to pursue their policy goals legislatively. However, because majority party status is strongly correlated with committee chair status, which is associated with more interbranch representation, estimating the effect of majority status becomes complicated. For the subset of legislators who are committee chairs, controlling for committee chair status could absorb any effect that majority party status grants on its own. Therefore, we present two versions of our models that test this hypothesis: one with controls for committee chair status and one without.
<!--Rochelle 11/14: if this isn't actually what's going on here, obviously pls rewrite this-->

#### Members of the House Majority do more General Policywork and Less Constituency Service 


The upper panels of @fig-marginal-majority shows the impact of majority status in the US House of Representatives. We focus first on the House, because House members experience the greatest change in their role and influence when their party wins and loses majority status. @fig-marginal-majority-1 shows the impact of majority status overall, while @fig-marginal-majority-2 shows the impact of majority status after controlling for committee leaderships positions---some of the mechanisms for how the majority wields its influence. We can think of that second model as capturing the impact of majority status for backbench member---i.e. those who do not hold a committee leadership position. We focus our attention on the diff-in-diff specification, which tells us the impact of a change to majority status holding constant the individual legislator. Consistent with our expectations, we find that when a legislator's party wins majority status in the House, they do less individual constituency service (-6%) and less nonprofit and local government service (-10%). Essentially, we see member of the minority party potentially prioritizing constituency service when they face greater obstacles in the legislative process (fewer votes, no agenda control, no committee chairs). Those effect sizes are fairly stable when we add committee leadership controls (individual constituency service: -6% to -5%; nonprofit and local government service -10% to -12%). 

```{r}
#| label: fig-marginal-majority
#| fig-cap: "Marginal Effect of Majority Status in the US House of Representatives. Points show the estimated percent difference in each type of interbranch representation, with 95% confidence intervals, from cross-sectional models."
#| fig-alt: "Marginal effects of majority status on five types of interbranch representation"
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "House Majority Status: No committee leadership controls"
#|   - "House Majority Status: Controls for commmittee leadership "
#|   - "Senate Majority Status: No committee leadership controls"
#|   - "Senate Majority Status: Controls for commmittee leadership "

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-majority-2.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-majority2-2.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-majority-3.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-majority2-3.png"))
```
<!--[DEVIN: check that I describing the models properly (i.e. didn't accidentally transpose which is which). ] --> 

Conversely, on the policy side, we see gaining majority status pushes legislators to do more general policy work. Interestingly, on the policy side, committee leadership controls have a large impact on the magnitude of the effect. Adding leadership controls cuts the effect of majority status on policy work nearly in half (+17% to 8.5%). This suggest that much of the extra policy work is done by committee chairs, consistent with our findings in @sec-results-capacity. Once we control for that extra policy work done by committee chairs in the majority, we see that the effect of majority status on the total interbranch work becomes significant. Members of the majority party do about 4% less total interbranch representation.  

We turn next to the story in the US Senate, represented by the lower panels in @fig-marginal-majority. We find no significant impact of majority status in any of our Senate models regardless of specification (cross sectional or diff-in-diff), or committee leadership controls. These stark differences in how the institutional environment shapes legislators strategic incentives between the House and Senate may surprise some readers, and there are a few explanations for why we may see them. Foremost among these explanations is the stark difference in the impact of majority status on the power of individual legislators between the chambers. The Senate continues to provide greater power to individual legislators through the filibuster and supermajority cloture requirements, which makes the switch between majority and minority status less salient absent supermajority control, which never occurs during our time period. For this reason we might expect the impact of majority status to be weaker for Senators than for House members. Another potential explanation is that there are many fewer US Senators than House members, which contributes to the much wider confidence intervals for our Senate estimates. 



### More Casework Staff, More Casework 

Finally, we turn to the mechanism of how member offices translate their priorities into action, by considering how they allocate their staff into different roles. @fig-staff-allocation shows the allocation of congressional staff across different role types over time. While the number of policy staff in member offices has gradually increased, we see no such change for constituent casework staff over time. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-staff-allocation
#| fig-cap: "Congressional Office Staff Allocation, 2011-2025"

here::here("figs", "staff-category-counts-over-time2-2.png") |>
  knitr::include_graphics() 
```



@fig-marginal-staff-allocation shows the marginal effect of an increase of one standard deviation in the number of constituency service staff members. We find that legislators who allocate more staff to constituency service do more constituency service. This pattern is true in both the House and the Senate. It also holds within legislators, so when legislators add more constituency service staff, we see them do more individual constituency service work. 


```{r}
#| label: fig-marginal-staff-allocation
#| fig-cap: "Marginal Effect of the Number of Casework Staff. Points show the estimated percent difference in each type of interbranch representation, with 95% confidence intervals, from cross-sectional models."
#| fig-alt: "Marginal effects of casework staff on five types of interbranch representation"
#| out-width: "100%"

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", "marginal-constituent-casework-staff-count-1.png"))
```

In considering our partisan and ideological incentives, on the whole we see *alignment* outweighing antagonism in shaping interbranch representation. Members of the president's party do more individual service, nonprofit/local government service, corporate policy and total interbranch representation. Similarly, those ideologically aligned with an agency do  more nonprofit service, general policy work, and total interbranch representation. We also see Republicans engaging in more corporate service work on behalf of their traditional business coalition. We also see anti-government Republicans (those in the Tea Party and Freedom Caucus) engaging in less policy work, and less total interbranch representation. 

But partisan and ideological alignment doesn't always win out. On the antagonist side, we see those that are ideologically distant from an agency engaging in more corporate policy work with that agency (think for example of  conservatives doing more corporate policy work with the EPA). We also see those anti-government Republicans in the House (Tea Party and Freedom Caucus members) engaging in more individual constituency service and corporate service---perhaps pushing back against a bureaucracy they loathe on behalf of their constituents. 

A surprising finding not linked to any of our hypotheses is that Republican legislators, including far-right Republicans who could be members of the Tea Party or Freedom Caucus, do more constituency service on behalf of individuals. We had expected far-right legislators to do less interbranch representation overall because of their general anti-government ideology, but this was not the case. One possible explanation for this relationship is that Republicans view individual constituency service as an opportunity to highlight the failures of government. For example, returning a large tax refund to a constituent from the IRS or helping a Social Security beneficiary receive delayed benefits would allow a Republican legislator to claim credit for helping constituents cut through "red tape" and receive what they are owed by the government as a taxpaying citizen. Testing this explanation is beyond the scope of our analysis here, but our findings still reveal a surprising way in which constituency service might be ideological or partisan, especially if this explanation is true. Interestingly, both parties, in theory, could claim to "own" constituency service as something that accords with their goals---while Republicans could describe their constituency service work as making sure that the federal government is not unfairly taking people's money or making things harder than necessary for individuals, Democrats could just as easily describe this kind of work as helping members of underserved communities get what they need from government. These unexpected findings provide an interesting contribution to the nascent literature on constituency service and partisanship, which has mostly examined that relationship from constituents' perspectives [e.g. @Wagner2007; @Snyder2024]. 

On the electoral side, despite the robust literature tying constituency service to re-election concerns, we see only a conditional relationship. We find that competitive general elections appear to help select legislators who do more service (from the cross-sectional model results), but competitive general elections don't change a legislators behavior. Instead, we see competitive primary elections, appearing to change behavior, where after a competitive primary House members do more constituency service. Surprisingly, given the greater competitiveness of Senate elections we see almost no relationship between electoral competitiveness and interbranch representation. The sole exception to that dynamic is that cross-sectionally, we see Senators from more competitive states doing less total interbranch representation, and less nonprofit and local government service. 

On the institutional side, we find interesting cross-chamber differences, consistent with each chamber's institutional rules. In the House, where Majority Status matters more, we see strong majority status effects in the difference-in-difference models, suggesting changed member behavior when their party moves into the majority. These new majority members do more general policy work---especially committee chairs, but they do less individual constituency service, nonprofit/local government service, and less total interbranch representation. This pattern is consistent with the idea that legislators who find themselves shut out of the lawmaking process while in the minority, may reallocate their efforts to activities like constituency service. On the Senate side, where the chamber operates more through either unanimous consent agreements, or super-majority cloture votes (3/5), we find majority status alone does not change behavior. 

Finally, we turn to our mechanism of constituency service staff. Consistent with our expectations we see that increasing the number of constituency service staff members increases the amount of individual constituency service work, and total interbranch representation work. Moreover, that finding holds within legislators. Somewhat surprisingly, we see that finding confined to individual constituency service, and we observe no increase in corporate or nonprofit/local government service when the number of constituency service staff is increased. 

## Conclusion: Incentives Shape Interbranch Representation

That the political environment would shape what politicians do may not be a surprising finding to any political scientist, but measuring and evaluating what incentives matter, and how they change behavior can tell us a lot. We find at least partial support for all of our strategic incentives hypotheses: partisan/ideological, electoral, and institutional, as well as support for our mechanism of staff allocation. 

Next, we'll attempt to zoom out, and discuss more broadly how our findings about demand, capacity, and strategic incentives change our understanding of congressional representation, and democratic governance more broadly [@sec-conclusion]. We also explore new questions about conceptualizing and measuring legislative effectiveness in Congress and whether our patterns of interbranch representation can be explained by variation in legislative styles. We conclude with considering practical implications of interbranch representation, how the casework to policy feedback loop can be improved, how interbranch representation might be changing under the second Trump administration and future areas of research.

#### Strategic responses to partisan institutions

A second component of legislators' strategic responses that may drive interbranch representation involves the partisan and ideological relationships between legislators and the executive branch. @tbl-models-full-1 shows that neither the party of the president, nor the ideological distance between a legislator and an agency, nor the interaction between these two variables is consistently related to individual constituency service. Sharing the president's party is positive and statistically significant only in Model 2 (the House and Senate difference-in-differences model). 


None of the other coefficients in the other models are significant at all, and the signs are inconsistent. We established two competing hypotheses in @sec-theory. On one hand, legislators may do more interbranch representation when they share the party of the president because they assume they are more likely to get a response (@thm-strategic-presidentmore); on the other hand, legislators may do more interbranch representation when they do *not* share the president's party because they will have a partisan incentive to conduct additional oversight of the bureaucracy (@thm-strategic-presidentless). We find support for neither hypothesis, which suggests that, for individual constituency service, legislators are not factoring partisanship or ideology into their work. This is consistent with our theoretical view of legislative offices as bureaucracies. 
 



```{r}
#| eval: false
#| label: fig-ideo-effect-1
#| fig-cap: "Predicted levels of interbranch representation compared to counterfactual of no difference in legislator ideology (a) and perceived agency ideology (b)"
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - ""
#|   - ""
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| out-width: 100%

knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", type, "m-ideo-effect-1.png"))
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", type, "m-ideo-effect-2.png"))
```

We had similar expectations regarding the respective ideologies of legislators and agencies and how that relationship might affect interbranch representation. Specifically, we hypothesized that legislators who are more ideologically proximate to an agency (and are therefore more likely to support its objectives) might send more letters to that agency (@thm-strategic-supportagency); alternatively, legislators who are more ideologically distant from an agency might send more letters to that agency as a means of conducting oversight (@thm-strategic-opposeagency). Our analysis finds no support for either of these hypotheses. Ideological distance between a legislator and an agency has no bearing on the amount of individual constituency service that a legislator does with that agency, as shown in Panel (b) of @fig-ideo-effect-1. Once again, the lack of ideological influence on constituent service speaks to a bureaucratic characterization of congressional offices.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", type, "m-partisan-effect-2.png"))
```


Although we had no specific hypotheses about how Democratic and Republican legislators may differ in the amount of individual constituency service that they provide as part of interbranch representation, Models 1 and 3 in @tbl-models-full-1 show that Republican members of the House did more constituent service on behalf of individuals. While these models show a large negative relationship between Independents and individual constituncy service, we do not see this in other specifications, such as a model with log population. It is also the case that legislators with more moderate voting records, as measured using the absolute values of their DW-NOMINATE scores, did more individual constituency service.
The impact of the latter variable on inequality is illustrated in Panel (a) of @fig-partisan-effect-1, which compares the predicted amounts of constituency service (based on legislator ideology) with a counterfactual in which ideology does not affect constituency service. In the counterfactual with no effect of legislator ideology, more ideologically extreme legislators would do more individual constituency service. Thus, we can see that more moderate legislators outperform their more ideologically extreme colleagues on this metric.
While consistent with assumptions about constituency service being the domain of ideological moderates, it is less clear how this behavior may reflect strategy on the part of moderate legislators, particularly given the inconsistent effects of electoral vulnerability discussed above.

#### Staff allocation reflects priorities


```{r}
#| eval: false
#| label: tbl-models-staff-1
#| tbl-cap: "The effect of staff budgeting on requests to federal agencies"
#| out-width: 100%

load(here::here("models", type,  "models_staff_spending.Rdata"))

modelsummary(models_staff_spending,
             notes = list("Robust standard errors in parentheses, clustered by legislator.",
                          "This table shows estimates of the effect of legislator staff spending. ")) 
```

Finally, we consider our last strategy-related hypothesis, which involves the allocation of staff. We operationalize legislators' staff allocations using the amount of their budget that they spend on legislative staff, communications staff, and constituency service staff. As established in @thm-strategic-staff, we expect that legislators who allocate more staff resources to constituency service will do more individual constituency service. We present these results in separate models, shown in @tbl-models-staff-1, because decisions about staff allocation are necessarily a function of many other variables included in our main models. Thus, Models 1 and 2 in @tbl-models-staff-1 include only our measures of staff spending (along with fixed effects), and Models 3 and 4 control for many of these other capacity-related factors. 


```{r}
#| eval: false
#| label: fig-effect-staff-1
#| fig-cap: "Predicted levels of interbranch representation per representative per year compared to counterfactual staffing levels"
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - ""
#|   - ""
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| out-width: 100%

knitr::include_graphics(
here::here("figs", type,
           paste0("m-staff_spending-effect-",
                  c(1:2), 
                  ".png"
                  ) 
           ))
```


Although the effects of staff budget allocation are not statistically significant in any of the models, it is useful to view counterfactual plots that show the magnitude of these effects. Constituent service staff spending does have a positive relationship with individual constituency service, as shown by Panel (a) of @fig-effect-staff-1. This figure compares the predicted amount of individual constituency service (based on our models) with the counterfactual that we would see if there were no effect of staff allocation. Across the distribution, legislators do more individual constituency service than they would in the counterfactual without the effect. A parallel effect exists for spending on communications staff, which has a negative relationship with individual constituency service. Panel (b) of @fig-effect-staff-1 shows that legislators would do *more* individual constituency service in a counterfactual without the effect of communications spending. Thus, while not statistically significant, these findings raise interesting questions about the relationship between staff allocation and interbranch representation. 



Surprisingly, we do not find a relationship between spending on constituency service staff and the volume of interbranch representation on behalf of individuals @thm-strategic-staff. Several factors may explain this. First, if a large share of constituency service staff time is dedicated to helping constituents register to vote or otherwise navigate non-federal bureaucracies, we may be missing this work. Second, constituency service staff may be classified .... 
It is also possible, as discussed above, that the *quality* of legislators' staff, rather than the *quantity*, matters. Legislators who are high performers on individual constituency service might possess small (or larger but underpaid) but dedicated and talented teams of caseworkers who are adept at navigating the federal bureaucracy in ways that are not captured by our measures.

#### Case Study: Energy PAC Campaign Contributions and Corporate Constituency Service to the Department of Energy

Up to this point in the chapter, we have examined the relationship between our framework of demand, capacity, and strategic choice and corporate constituency service work with all federal agencies. Before concluding the chapter and moving on to the next form of interbranch representation, we present a case study of corporate constituency service directed toward the Department of Energy. By focusing on work with a single agency, we can look more specifically at campaign contributions the legislator received from the energy sector political action committees (as opposed to the total corporate PAC contributions we examined in the previous section and models). @tbl-models-pac-energy-2 uses a similar model specification as @tbl-models-pac-2, but changes the dependent variable to corporate constituency service to the Department of Energy. 

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| label: tbl-models-pac-energy-2
#| tbl-cap: "Corporate Constituency Service requests to the Department of Energy and Energy Sector Political Action Committee Contributions in the Prior Congress" 

load(here::here("models", type,  "models_pac_energy.Rdata"))

modelsummary(models_pac_energy,
             notes = list("Robust standard errors in parentheses, clustered by district",
                          "This table shows estimates of the relationship between corporate Political Action Committee donations and levels of interbranch representation.")) 
```
\clearpage 

Just as with the aggregate data across all agencies (@tbl-models-pac-2), we find that prior contributions from the energy sector are positively correlated with corporate service in the cross-sectional models, but not in the difference-in-difference models. This pattern of contributions mattering in cross-sectional models but not differences in difference models would be consistent with a story of corporate donors giving to like-minded members, rather than contributions changing behavior. Other interpretations, of course, are possible given ambiguities of temporal sequencing and the limitations of what we can say with this research design. 

Ellie: How do we want to interpret that difference? My intuition: contributions given to members with pro-industry views, rather than contributions causing changes in behavior.

#### Interbranch representation as electoral strategy

We find no support for our expectations in @thm-strategic-election that legislators facing more competitive elections would do more interbranch representation. The coefficient for the variable capturing competitive general elections is statistically significant only in Model 3 (Senate only). Contrary to our expectations, then, senators facing *less* competitive general elections do more constituency service on behalf of nonprofits and local governments.

#### Strategic responses to partisan institutions

Consistent with our expectations in @thm-strategic-presidentmore, we find that legislators who share the president's party do more constituency service on behalf of nonprofit organizations and local governments. The rationale behind this hypothesis was that legislators might anticipate a greater likelihood of receiving a response from an agency that is part of a friendly presidential administration. Our competing hypothesis, @thm-strategic-presidentless, posited that legislators would likely do more interbranch representation when they do *not* share the president's party because they would have a partisan incentive to conduct oversight. For this specific type of interbranch representation, in which legislators are mostly writing in support of nonprofit organizations and local governments applying for grants from the federal government, finding support for @thm-strategic-presidentmore makes sense. It may also be the case that legislators are more likely to write in support of applications to grants that are part of programs they support. A co-partisan presidential administration would be more likely to implement such programs. Where possible, a more in-depth analysis of specific grants mentioned in the letters would shed light on this potential mechanism. Panel (a) in @fig-partisan-effect-3 shows how sharing the president's party contributes to the inequality in this type of interbranch representation that we find across legislators.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figs", type, "m-partisan-effect-2.png"))
```

Our hypotheses regarding ideological distance between legislators and agencies followed similar logic. On one hand, we expected that legislators may do more interbranch representation with agencies to which they are ideologically proximate, the argument being that they support the agency's objectives (@thm-strategic-supportagency). On the other hand, we posited that legislators may do more interbranch representation with agencies from which they are ideologically distant, as they may actively oppose the agency's objectives (@thm-strategic-opposeagency). We find support for @thm-strategic-supportagency. Legislators do more constituency service on behalf of nonprofits and local governments with ideologically proximate agencies. Again, this pattern may speak to the fact that legislators support the overall policy objectives of the grants for which these constituent groups are applying, particularly because the analyses for individual and corporate constituency service in the previous two chapters do not support this hypothesis. It is also worth noting that Democrats do more of this type of interbranch representation than Republicans and Independents, consistent with Democrats' higher levels of support for government spending and other programs.

The effect of legislators' ideology on interbranch representation is consistent with the results from previous chapters. More ideologically moderate legislators do more interbranch representation on behalf of nonprofits and local governments. @fig-ideo-effect-3 shows the effect of ideological extremity on the inequality in this form of interbranch representation that we observe across legislators (Panel (a)), as well as the effect of agency ideology on this inequality (Panel (b)). As we can see from the comparisons between each effect and the counterfactuals in which these effects are not present, both of these factors impact inequality across legislators. However, that impact is larger for legislators' ideology. 

#### Staff allocation reflects priorities


Next we consider how legislators' decisions about staff allocation might affect the amount of interbranch representation that they provide. @tbl-models-staff-3 shows the results of models using legislators' staff budgets in three different categories--legislative staff, communications staff, and constituency service staff--as the main independent variables. Models 1 and 2 examine the effects of these variables on their own (with fixed effects), while Models 3 and 4 also control for elements of capacity and strategy. All models examine House members only. We focus on the cross-sectional results in Models 1 and 3.

```{r}
#| out-width: 100%
```
